summary: Extends IS-IS Traffic Engineering (RFC 5305) to distribute network-performance information, such as latency, in a scalable way. This matters in networks like financial data networks where such measures matter as much as other metrics for path selection. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Some networks care more about how fast traffic crosses a link than how many hops it takes. This document lets IS-IS routers advertise what they measure about their links, so that path selection elsewhere in the network can take latency, loss and spare capacity into account.

questions: what is is-is te metric extensions
what is the anomalous bit in is-is
subtitle: Letting IS-IS carry latency, loss and bandwidth measurements between routers.

tldr.problem: In some networks, such as financial data networks, latency matters as much as any other metric for choosing a path, but IS-IS Traffic Engineering had no way to distribute performance data.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8570 defines seven new sub-TLVs, types 33 to 39, carrying link delay, minimum and maximum delay, delay variation, loss, residual, available and utilized bandwidth, plus rules for thresholds, throttling and an Anomalous bit.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 7810 and fixes an ambiguity in the length of the bandwidth sub-TLVs. It only distributes the data; measuring it and acting on it are out of scope.

today: RFC 8570 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2019. It obsoletes RFC 7810 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard way for IS-IS to advertise link performance measurements.

sections.title: Why Latency Became a Routing Metric
sections.content:
In certain networks, such as financial information networks like stock market data providers, network-performance information such as latency is becoming as critical to data-path selection as other metrics. In these networks, extremely large amounts of money rest on the ability to access market data in real time and to predictably make trades faster than the competition. Because of this, using metrics such as hop count or cost as routing metrics is becoming only tangentially important. It would be more useful to make path-selection decisions based on performance data such as latency, in a cost-effective and scalable way.

This document describes extensions, called the IS-IS TE Metric Extensions, to the Extended IS Reachability TLV defined in RFC 5305. These extensions can be used to distribute network-performance information: link delay, delay variation, packet loss, residual bandwidth and available bandwidth.

The data distributed is meant to be used as part of the operation of the routing protocol, for example by replacing cost with latency or considering bandwidth as well as cost, to enhance Constrained Shortest Path First, or for other uses such as supplementing the data used by an Application-Layer Traffic Optimization server. With respect to Constrained Shortest Path First, the data can be used to set up, fail over and fail back data paths using protocols such as RSVP-TE.

The mechanisms described only disseminate performance information. The methods for initially gathering it, such as those in RFC 6375, and how to act on it once it is distributed, are outside the scope of the document. Example mechanisms to measure latency, delay variation and loss in an MPLS network are given in RFC 6374. While the document does not specify how the performance information should be obtained, the measurement of delay SHOULD NOT vary significantly based on the offered traffic load, so queuing delays SHOULD NOT be included in the delay measurement. For links such as forwarding adjacencies, care must be taken that the measurement avoids significant queuing delays, which could be done by measuring with a traffic class that experiences minimal queuing, or by summing the measured link delays of the components of the link's path.
sections.plainLanguage: In a network that carries market data, a few milliseconds of extra delay can cost money, so the number of hops stops being the interesting measure. This document lets routers publish what they measure about their own links, so that the rest of the network can choose paths on speed instead.

sections.title: The Seven New Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The document registers new IS-IS TE sub-TLVs in the registry of sub-TLVs for TLVs 22, 23, 141, 222 and 223, and they build on the extensions provided in IS-IS Traffic Engineering and GMPLS. The Extended IS Reachability TLV, type 22, the Inter-AS Reachability TLV, type 141, and the MT-ISN TLV, type 222, all have nested sub-TLVs that permit the TLVs to be readily extended. The new sub-TLVs are type 33 Unidirectional Link Delay, 34 Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay, 35 Unidirectional Delay Variation, 36 Unidirectional Link Loss, 37 Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth, 38 Unidirectional Available Bandwidth and 39 Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth.

The new sub-TLVs include a bit called the Anomalous bit, or A bit. When the A bit is clear, or when the sub-TLV does not include an A bit, the sub-TLV describes steady-state link performance, which could be used to construct a steady-state performance topology for initial tunnel-path computation or to verify alternative failover paths.

When network performance violates configurable link-local thresholds, a sub-TLV with the A bit set is advertised. That sub-TLV could be used by the receiving node to determine whether to fail traffic to a backup path or to calculate an entirely new path. From an MPLS perspective, the intent of the A bit is to permit label switched path ingress nodes to determine whether the link referenced in the sub-TLV affects any of the label switched paths for which it is ingress. If they are affected, the node can determine whether those paths still meet end-to-end performance objectives, and if not, it can move affected traffic to a pre-established protection path or establish a new path and place the traffic in it.

If link performance then improves beyond a configurable minimum value, the reuse threshold, the sub-TLV can be re-advertised with the A bit cleared, and a receiving node can do whatever re-optimization or failback it wishes, including nothing. A sub-TLV that does not include the A bit cannot be used for failover purposes; the A bit was intentionally omitted from some sub-TLVs to help mitigate oscillations.

Consistent with the existing IS-IS TE specification, the bandwidth advertisements MUST be encoded as IEEE floating-point values, while the delay and delay-variation advertisements MUST be encoded as integer values. Delay values MUST be quantified in units of microseconds, packet loss MUST be quantified as a percentage of packets sent, and bandwidth MUST be sent as bytes per second. All values, except residual bandwidth, MUST be calculated as rolling averages, where the averaging period MUST be a configurable period of time.
sections.plainLanguage: Each measurement travels in its own small record nested inside the reachability record that the router already advertises. A single bit in most of them says whether the link is behaving normally or has gone outside the thresholds the operator set, which is what tells a receiving router that it may need to move traffic.

sections.title: What Each Sub-TLV Carries
sections.content:
The Unidirectional Link Delay sub-TLV, type 33, advertises the average link delay between two directly connected IS-IS neighbours. The delay advertised MUST be the delay from the local neighbour to the remote one, that is the forward-path latency. It is four octets long and carries a 24-bit delay value in microseconds as an integer. When set to the maximum value 16,777,215, that is 16.777215 seconds, the delay is at least that value and may be larger.

The Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay sub-TLV, type 34, advertises the minimum and maximum delay values between two directly connected neighbours, each as a 24-bit integer in microseconds. It is eight octets long. The two values may be the same, and either may again carry the maximum value. Implementations MAY also permit the configuration of an offset value in microseconds to be added to the measured delay, to communicate operator-specific delay constraints.

The Unidirectional Delay Variation sub-TLV, type 35, advertises the average link delay variation, again forward-path, as a 24-bit integer in microseconds. It has no A bit, and a value of 0 means it has not been measured.

The Unidirectional Link Loss sub-TLV, type 36, advertises the loss as a packet percentage between two directly connected neighbours, forward-path. The 24-bit field carries link packet loss as a percentage of the total traffic sent over a configurable interval, where the basic unit is 0.000003%, so that 2^24 - 2 is 50.331642%. That is the highest packet-loss percentage that can be expressed, on the assumptions that precision matters more on high-speed links than advertising larger loss rates, and that high-speed links with over 50% loss are unusable. Measured values larger than the field maximum SHOULD be encoded as the maximum value.

The Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 37, advertises the residual bandwidth from the system originating the advertisement to its neighbour, in IEEE floating-point format with units of bytes per second. For a link or forwarding adjacency, residual bandwidth is the maximum bandwidth minus the bandwidth currently allocated to RSVP-TE label switched paths; for a bundled link it is the sum of the component link residual bandwidths. This differs from unreserved bandwidth, which is subtracted from the maximum reservable bandwidth and gives per-priority remainders, while residual bandwidth subtracts tunnel reservations from the link capacity and gives an aggregated remainder across priorities. The two can be used concurrently, each with its own use case, the former for applications such as Weighted ECMP and the latter for call admission control.

The Unidirectional Available Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 38, advertises the available bandwidth from the system originating it, in the same units. For a link or forwarding adjacency it is the residual bandwidth minus the measured bandwidth used for the actual forwarding of non-RSVP-TE packets; for a bundled link it is the sum of the component link available bandwidths.

The Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth sub-TLV, type 39, advertises the bandwidth utilization from the system originating it, in the same units. For a link or forwarding adjacency it is the actual utilization of the link as measured by the advertising node; for a bundled link it is the sum of the component link utilizations.

The use of these sub-TLVs is not confined to the traffic engineering context: they can also be used for computing paths in the absence of a traffic engineering subsystem. As in the traffic engineering case, the Interface Address and Neighbor Address sub-TLVs, IPv4 or IPv6, MUST be present.
sections.plainLanguage: There are seven measurements: average delay, the slowest and fastest delay seen, how much the delay wobbles, how many packets are lost, how much capacity is left after tunnels are booked, how much capacity is left after ordinary traffic, and how much capacity is in use. Delays are in microseconds, loss is a percentage, and capacity is in bytes per second.

sections.title: Thresholds and Announcement Timing
sections.content:
The values advertised in all sub-TLVs, except minimum and maximum delay and residual bandwidth, MUST represent an average over a period of time, or be obtained by a filter that is reasonably representative of an average, for example a rolling average. Minimum and maximum delay MUST each be derived either by taking the lowest and highest measured value over a measurement interval, or by using a filter or other technique that gives a reasonable representation of a minimum and a maximum for the interval, with compensation for outliers. The measurement interval, any filter coefficients and any advertisement intervals MUST be configurable per sub-TLV.

In addition to the measurement intervals governing re-advertisement, implementations SHOULD provide configurable accelerated advertisement thresholds per sub-TLV. The advertisement is made immediately if the measured parameter falls outside a configured upper bound, for all but the minimum delay metric, where a lower bound applies instead, and the advertised sub-TLV is not already outside that bound, or if the difference between the last advertised value and the current measured value exceeds a configured threshold. For sub-TLVs that include an A bit, an additional threshold SHOULD be included, corresponding to the point at which performance is considered anomalous and sub-TLVs with the A bit are sent; the A bit is cleared when the performance has been below, or has re-crossed, that threshold for one or more advertisement intervals, to permit failback.

To prevent oscillations, only the high threshold or the low threshold, but not both, may be used to trigger any given sub-TLV that supports both. Once outside the bounds of the threshold, any re-advertisement of a measurement within the bounds remains governed solely by the measurement interval for that sub-TLV.

When link performance values change by small amounts that fall under the thresholds, implementations SHOULD suppress sub-TLV re-advertisement and lengthen the period within which the sub-TLVs are refreshed. Only the accelerated advertisement threshold mechanism may shorten the re-advertisement interval, and all suppression and re-advertisement interval backoff timer features SHOULD be configurable.
sections.plainLanguage: Measurements are averaged before they are published, so a single hiccup does not move the number. A router only republishes immediately when a value crosses a limit the operator set or moves by more than a set amount; otherwise it waits for the next scheduled update. Two limits cannot both trigger the same record, or the number would flap up and down.

sections.title: Keeping the Network Stable
sections.content:
The configurable mechanisms described earlier bound the number of re-advertisements. Instability might occur in very large networks if measurement intervals are set low enough to overwhelm the processing of flooded information at some of the routers in the topology, so care should be taken in setting these values. The default measurement interval for all sub-TLVs SHOULD be 30 seconds.

Announcements MUST also be able to be throttled using configurable inter-update throttle timers. The minimum announcement periodicity is one announcement per second, and the default value SHOULD be set to 120 seconds. Implementations SHOULD NOT permit the inter-update timer to be lower than the measurement interval. It is also RECOMMENDED that the underlying performance-measurement mechanisms not include any significant buffer delay, any significant buffer-induced delay variation, or any significant loss due to buffer overflow or due to active queue management.
sections.plainLanguage: Publishing a measurement on every small change would flood a large network with updates, so there are floors: measure over at least half a minute by default, and publish at most once a second, with two minutes as the usual interval.

sections.title: Turning Measurements On and Off
sections.content:
Implementations MUST make it possible to individually enable or disable each sub-TLV based on configuration. They SHOULD also permit static configuration and manual override of the dynamic measurements for each sub-TLV, in order to simplify migration and to mitigate scenarios where dynamic measurements are not possible.

As in RFC 5305, unrecognized sub-TLVs should be silently ignored.

The document also records what changed from RFC 7810. Errata ID 5293 identified that in RFC 7810 the length associated with the residual, available and utilized bandwidth sub-TLVs did not match the figures, because the specified length of 4 did not include the RESERVED field shown in them. Investigation showed that some implementations had used the length of 4 and omitted the field, while others included the field and used a length of 5, and since those choices are not interoperable, a new version was needed. The choice made here is to omit the unused RESERVED field from these sub-TLVs and use the length of 4, which matches the corresponding advertisements in the equivalent OSPF traffic engineering specification and in the BGP Link State specification. Errata ID 5486 also identified that the definition of available bandwidth on bundled links used a circular definition, using the sum of the component link available bandwidths where it should have used the sum of the component link residual bandwidths; this has been corrected and clarified.
sections.plainLanguage: Each measurement can be switched on or off separately, and an operator can type in a value instead of a measured one, which helps when moving to the new records. The document also sorts out a mismatch in the length of the bandwidth records that had made two kinds of implementation unable to talk to each other.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The sub-TLVs introduced in this document allow an operator to advertise state information of links, such as bandwidth and delay, that could be sensitive and that an operator may not want to disclose. The mechanism for ensuring network stability when the new sub-TLVs are advertised is described earlier, and implementations SHOULD follow those guidelines to mitigate the risk of instability.

RFC 5304 describes an authentication method for IS-IS link state PDUs that allows cryptographic authentication of them. It is anticipated that in most deployments the IS-IS protocol is used within an infrastructure entirely under the control of the same operator. It is still worth considering that the effect of sending traffic engineering sub-TLVs over insecure links could include a man-in-the-middle attacker delaying real-time data to a given site or destination, which could negatively affect the value of the data for that site or destination. The use of link state PDU cryptographic authentication allows the risk of such attacks to be mitigated.
sections.plainLanguage: The measurements describe how busy each link is, and an operator may not want that published to anyone who can see the routing protocol. Where it matters, the existing IS-IS authentication can be used to protect the advertisements.

items.label: Unidirectional Link Delay
items.desc: Average link delay in microseconds. Length 4, with an A bit.

items.label: Min/Max Unidirectional Link Delay
items.desc: Lowest and highest delay measured, in microseconds. Length 8, with an A bit.

items.label: Unidirectional Delay Variation
items.desc: Average delay variation in microseconds. Length 4, no A bit.

items.label: Unidirectional Link Loss
items.desc: Packet loss as a percentage. Length 4, with an A bit.

items.label: Unidirectional Residual Bandwidth
items.desc: Maximum bandwidth minus what RSVP-TE tunnels have reserved. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Available Bandwidth
items.desc: Residual bandwidth minus what other traffic is using. Length 4.

items.label: Unidirectional Utilized Bandwidth
items.desc: The measured bandwidth in use on the link. Length 4.

fields.name: A bit and reserved
fields.desc: The A bit is set when the measured value exceeds its configured maximum threshold, and cleared when it falls below the reuse threshold.

fields.name: Delay
fields.desc: The average link delay over a configurable interval in microseconds. The maximum value 16,777,215 means the delay is at least that.

cells: The maximum bandwidth, that is the link capacity

viz.caption: WHEN A MEASUREMENT IS PUBLISHED AGAIN

items.title: Measurement interval
items.text: Values must be averages over a period, or a filter that is representative of an average. The default should be 30 seconds.

items.title: Out of bounds
items.text: If the measured value falls outside a configured bound, and the advertised value is not already outside it, the advertisement is made immediately.

items.title: Changed enough
items.text: If the difference between the last advertised value and the current measurement exceeds a configured threshold, the advertisement is made immediately.

items.title: No oscillation
items.text: Only the high or the low threshold, not both, may trigger a given sub-TLV, and once outside the bounds a re-advertisement waits for the measurement interval.
